authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro — unreviewed candidate generation

items.prompt: All values and target T are positive. While seeking the shortest nonempty range with sum at least T, the current window first reaches sum ≥ T. What should the shrink rule do?
constraints: Every value is positive.
T is positive.
Only nonempty ranges are answer candidates.
The objective is minimum length.

options.text: Record the current length, remove the leftmost value, and repeat while the sum remains at least T.
Stop shrinking after the first valid window because it is already the earliest ending at this right boundary.
Remove values only until the global best length changes.
Clear the entire window after recording one valid range.

feedback.reason: For a shortest objective, every valid left removal produces a shorter candidate ending at the same right boundary.

blocks.text: Positivity makes each left removal decrease the sum. Once expansion reaches validity, the algorithm should test the current length, remove one left value, and continue while the threshold still holds. The final valid state before the sum drops below T is the shortest candidate ending at this right boundary. Stopping after one candidate can miss a shorter one, and clearing the range discards overlap needed for later endings. The loop condition is validity, not whether the global answer happened to change.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.stop_at_first_valid: The first valid window for this right boundary is usually the longest of the valid suffixes, not the shortest.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.shrink_until_answer_changes: The answer may remain unchanged even though more left removals are required to find the locally minimal valid candidate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reset_window: A full reset discards starts that can combine with future values and is not justified by the monotone invariant.

items.prompt: A window tracks nonnegative costs under a nonnegative budget B and must keep total cost at most B while maximizing length. After adding a value makes the window invalid, which rule is correct?
constraints: All costs are nonnegative.
B is nonnegative.
Validity is totalCost ≤ B.
The objective is maximum length.

options.text: Record the over-budget length first, then shrink once.
Advance left and remove costs while totalCost > B; once valid, consider the resulting length.
Keep shrinking while totalCost ≤ B.
Move the right boundary backward until the prior window is restored.

feedback.reason: For a longest-valid objective, invalid state must be repaired before the current range can update the answer.

blocks.text: With nonnegative costs, removing values from the left cannot increase total cost, so repeated left moves eventually restore totalCost ≤ B. After repair, the remaining window is the longest valid suffix ending at the current right boundary because any earlier left position was still invalid when removed. Recording the over-budget range scores an illegal candidate; shrinking while already valid discards length without need; moving right backward breaks the one-pass monotone traversal. Zero-cost removals preserve rather than reduce total cost, but left still advances; nonnegative state direction and pointer progress keep the repair rule sound.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.record_invalid_then_shrink: The current length violates the budget and cannot be compared with valid answers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.shrink_while_valid: This rule belongs to minimum-length at-least-threshold objectives; here it would throw away valid length.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.move_right_back: A legal monotone window never needs to retract the right boundary; left repairs the current ending.

items.prompt: For a nonnegative budget B, which condition is sufficient for the standard one-pass window that finds the longest contiguous range with sum at most B?
constraints: The algorithm only moves left and right forward.
B is nonnegative.
It repairs an over-budget sum by removing values from the left.

options.text: Every value is distinct.
Values are sorted in ascending order.
Every value is nonnegative, so expansion cannot reduce the sum and left removal cannot increase it.
Every value is an integer, possibly negative.

feedback.reason: Nonnegative values make the budget-validity predicate monotone under the two boundary moves.

blocks.text: The repair rule assumes that an over-budget window cannot become valid by expanding farther and can become valid by removing a prefix. Nonnegative values provide both facts: adding cannot lower the sum, and removing cannot raise it. Distinctness and sorted order do not guarantee those directional effects if negative values are present. Integer type alone is irrelevant. The same precondition supports shortest-at-least sum windows, with the valid/invalid shrink regime adjusted to the objective.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.distinct_values: Distinct values can still be negative, so the sum may move in the wrong direction for a safe discard rule.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_values: A sorted sequence may contain negative values; ordering by value does not make boundary removal monotone for every window.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.integer_values: Signed integers allow expansion and shrinkage to change the sum in either direction.

items.prompt: A positive-value shortest-sum window is applied unchanged to [1, -1, 5] with T = 5. It reaches sum 5 for the whole range, records length 3, removes 1, gets sum 4, and stops shrinking. Why does it miss the optimal range [5]?
constraints: The attempted algorithm stops shrinking as soon as the current sum is below T.
Negative values are allowed in this trace.

options.text: The right boundary must move backward after every failed shrink.
The only issue is using r − l instead of r − l + 1.
The window method works only when T exceeds every individual value.
Removing the next left value −1 would increase the sum from 4 to 5, so ‘currently invalid’ does not imply that further shrinking stays invalid.

feedback.reason: A negative outgoing value reverses the assumed shrink direction: removing it can increase the sum and restore validity.

blocks.text: The positive-value algorithm stops when one removal makes sum < T because, with nonnegative values, every later removal can only decrease or preserve the sum. Here the next outgoing value is −1. Removing it raises the sum from 4 to 5 and exposes the length-1 valid range [5]. The algorithm therefore discarded the possibility by treating invalidity as monotone under further shrinkage.

blocks.title: General signed boundary
blocks.text: For the general shortest-at-least problem with signed values, a standard alternative combines prefix sums with a monotonic deque: the deque stores candidate start boundaries in increasing prefix-sum order, removes older tail candidates when the current later prefix is no larger and therefore dominates them, and removes front candidates when the current-prefix difference reaches T. That mechanism does not assume one left pointer remains safe.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.right_must_move_backward: The missed candidate already ends at the current right boundary; the failure is the unsafe stopping rule for left moves.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.length_formula_wrong: An off-by-one error would change reported lengths but would not explain why the [5] candidate is never examined.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_too_small: The relation between T and individual values is not the required precondition; the sign of contributions controls monotonicity.

items.prompt: For a longest window with nonnegative total cost at most 10, adding the next value raises the sum to 15. Removing the leftmost value 2 leaves sum 13. Why must the repair use a while loop rather than a single if?
constraints: The objective allows a variable window length.
The window is valid only when sum ≤ 10.

options.text: One removal may leave the invariant violated, so left must continue moving until sum ≤ 10.
A while loop is required only because each iteration must improve the global answer.
The sum 15 proves the incoming value was added twice.
An if statement is never correct in any sliding-window algorithm.

feedback.reason: A variable window has no guarantee that one outgoing element is enough to restore its validity invariant.

blocks.text: The invalid state is sum=15 and the first removal yields 13, which is still over budget. The algorithm must keep removing left contributions until the maintained state is legal. The loop is controlled by validity, not by answer changes. An if can be correct for a fixed-size slide where exactly one excess element exists, but not for a general variable constraint that may require several repairs after one expansion. After every removal, state must be updated before the condition is checked again; otherwise the loop can stop on stale invalidity or remove too much.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.while_improves_answer: Repair iterations may not improve the answer at all; they are required to re-establish a legal state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.right_added_twice: A legitimate large incoming value can create a sum of 15; the trace gives no evidence of duplicate addition.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.if_is_never_valid: Fixed-size windows commonly need at most one removal per expansion. The issue is the variable validity condition, not the syntax itself.

items.prompt: The shortest-sum-at-least-T window is changed from strictly positive values to nonnegative values that may include zero. Does the same monotonic shrink rule remain valid?
constraints: No value is negative.
The left boundary advances on every shrink iteration, even when the removed value is zero.

options.text: No. A zero means the sum does not change, so the algorithm can never make progress.
Yes. Expansion cannot decrease the sum and removal cannot increase it; zeros may preserve the sum but do not reverse the direction.
Only if all zeros appear before positive values.
Zeros permit only a fixed-size window, never a variable one.

feedback.reason: Nonnegative values preserve the directional sum invariant; pointer movement, not strict sum change, guarantees progress through zeros.

blocks.text: Strict positivity is stronger than necessary for correctness. With zeros, adding still never lowers the sum and removing still never raises it. A shrink iteration that removes zero may leave the sum unchanged, but left advances, so the algorithm cannot loop forever and can expose a shorter candidate with the same sum. The boundary fails only when a negative value can reverse the effect. This transfer sharpens the precondition from ‘positive’ to the materially sufficient ‘nonnegative’.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_zero_breaks: The state need not change on every iteration; the left index changes, so the candidate becomes shorter and the loop progresses.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_if_sorted: The location of zeros does not affect the nonnegative direction of additions and removals.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_fixed_size: Variable windows work with zero contributions as long as the validity predicate remains monotone and pointer progress is explicit.

items.prompt: A longest-valid window receives a new right value and violates its predicate. What is the correct immediate response when left-removal is proven monotone?

options.text: Remove outgoing left contributions and advance left while invalid, then score the restored-valid window.
Record the expanded range first because it is longer than every repaired range.
Discard the entire window and restart at right+1 regardless of the predicate.
Move right backward until the previous window becomes valid.

feedback.reason: The monotonic proof makes left-shrink the safe repair and longest scoring occurs only after validity is restored.

blocks.text: Update state for the entering value, then repeatedly remove the oldest contribution while the predicate is violated. Once valid, the current interval is the longest candidate for this right endpoint because earlier starts were either retained or safely discarded. Recording before repair accepts an invalid range.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.record_invalid: The answer contract requires a valid window.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reset_all: A proven shrink rule can preserve earlier valid starts and need not discard the whole range.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.move_right_back: Right normally advances through input; repair removes from the left.

items.prompt: For a shortest window whose sum is at least T with positive values, when should the algorithm update the best length during shrinking?

options.text: Record the current valid length before each removal, then remove left and continue while the predicate remains true.
Record only after the removal makes the sum fall below T.
Record only immediately after right expands and never during repair.
Keep the maximum length because every valid range is a candidate for the shortest objective.

feedback.reason: With positive values, each shrink can produce a shorter still-valid range, and the optimum may occur just before validity is lost.

blocks.text: When sum≥T, record the current length, remove the leftmost value, update state, and repeat. The first invalid state cannot be used, so recording only after invalidity misses the last valid candidate. The objective's direction changes answer-update timing even though the same shrink proof applies.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.record_after_invalid: The range after removal may be invalid, and the preceding valid length may be the optimum.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.record_expanded_only: A shorter valid suffix can emerge during repeated shrinkage.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.record_longest: The task minimizes length, so retaining the maximum reverses the objective.

items.prompt: Which fact supports linear total boundary movement in a one-pass variable window?

options.text: right advances at most n times and left also advances at most n times, never moving backward.
The code has one outer loop, so the inner while cannot add asymptotic work.
Positive values alone prove O(n) even if left can move backward.
Every variable window has constant length after the first expansion.

feedback.reason: Amortized linearity follows from monotone, bounded movement of each boundary, not from loop nesting syntax.

blocks.text: Although the while loop can execute many times for one right endpoint, every removal advances left and each element leaves at most once. With n right advances and n left advances, total boundary updates are O(n). The validity proof is separate from this runtime proof.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_outer_loop: A nested loop can be quadratic when the inner index repeatedly revisits positions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.positive_values_only: Positivity helps prove shrink legality, but O(n) also needs bounded monotone movement.

items.prompt: Select all facts that should trigger a review before transferring a positive-sum shortest-window proof to a new problem.

options.text: The new input admits negative values.
The validity condition is not known to be monotone under removing the leftmost element.
The new problem retains positive values and the same threshold predicate.
The new code uses left and right variables with the same names.

feedback.reason: The proof depends on value signs and predicate behavior, not the surface shape of the loop.

blocks.text: A transfer is safe when the premises that make removal monotone and discarded starts irrelevant remain true. Negative values or a nonmonotone predicate invalidate that inference and require a different proof or method. Retaining the same positive domain and threshold supports transfer; names do not.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_positive_domain: This preserves the key premise rather than blocking transfer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_boundary_names: Variable names carry no correctness theorem.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.signed_values: Removing an outgoing negative can increase the sum and future negatives can rescue old starts.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.different_predicate: A while-loop condition is insufficient without a monotonic restoration argument.

items.prompt: Why is positivity a key precondition for the standard shortest-subarray-with-sum-at-least-target window?
constraints: Every array value is strictly positive.
The target is fixed.

options.text: Expanding never decreases the sum and shrinking never increases it, so the validity predicate changes monotonically.
options.explanation: This justifies advancing each boundary once.

options.text: Positive values make every frequency map monotone under both pointer moves.
options.explanation: The proof concerns numeric sum, not frequencies.

options.text: Positivity makes sorting unnecessary for all subarray objectives.
options.explanation: It does not solve unrelated output geometries.

options.text: Positive sums cannot overflow because they never decrease.
options.explanation: Magnitude can still exceed the numeric type.

feedback.reason: Positivity supplies the one-way relation between endpoint movement and sum validity.

blocks.text: With positive values, expansion can only help reach the threshold and shrinking can only reduce the sum. This makes the inner shrink loop amortized linear; signed values remove that guarantee.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.frequency_monotone: The proof concerns numeric sum, not frequencies.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorting_free: It does not solve unrelated output geometries.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_overflow: Magnitude can still exceed the numeric type.

items.prompt: Why must a shortest-valid window shrink in a `while` loop rather than a single `if` after it first becomes valid?
constraints: Several leftmost elements may be removable while validity remains true.
The objective is minimum length.

options.text: Repeatedly remove the leftmost item and update the answer until the next removal would make the window invalid.
options.explanation: The shortest valid suffix may require multiple removals.

options.text: One removal always reaches the shortest valid window because the first valid state is minimal.
options.explanation: The first valid window can contain multiple redundant positives.

options.text: Expand before removing anything so the next candidate is always longer.
options.explanation: That moves away from the minimum objective.

options.text: Reset left to zero after validity so every prefix is checked again.
options.explanation: Resetting destroys the monotone pointer proof.

feedback.reason: The minimum may lie several positions inside the first valid window.

blocks.text: The algorithm records each valid length during the inner loop. It stops at the first invalid removal, where the last recorded boundary is the shortest valid suffix for that right endpoint.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_removal_enough: The first valid window can contain multiple redundant positives.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.expand_again: That moves away from the minimum objective.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reset_left: Resetting destroys the monotone pointer proof.

items.prompt: At what point should a shortest-valid window update the global minimum during shrink?
constraints: The current window is valid.
The next removal may make it invalid.

options.text: Record the current valid length before removing its leftmost element, then test the next state.
options.explanation: The current window is a legal candidate even if the next one is not.

options.text: Remove first and record the length even when the new window is invalid.
Update only immediately after adding a rightmost element.
options.explanation: The best window often appears after one or more left removals.

options.text: Wait until the entire scan ends and keep only the final valid window.
options.explanation: Earlier right endpoints may produce the global optimum.

feedback.reason: The answer update must happen while the predicate still holds.

blocks.text: A shrink step can cross the validity boundary. Recording before that step preserves the last legal candidate; recording afterward would either miss it or store an invalid range.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.record_expansion_only: The best window often appears after one or more left removals.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.record_at_end: Earlier right endpoints may produce the global optimum.

items.prompt: Why is the standard positive-sum variable window O(n) despite a nested shrink loop?
constraints: The right pointer advances from left to right once.
The left pointer never moves backward.

options.text: Each element enters the window once and leaves at most once, so total pointer advances are O(n).
options.explanation: Nested syntax does not imply a multiplicative full scan.

options.text: The shrink loop is constant time because it runs only once per input.
options.explanation: It can run many times, but the total is amortized.

options.text: Sorting makes the nested loop linear after preprocessing.
options.explanation: The standard algorithm need not sort, and sorting adds cost.

options.text: Random access lets the algorithm skip every removed element without charging it.
options.explanation: The proof charges each actual pointer movement once.

feedback.reason: Amortized analysis counts total monotone pointer movement rather than multiplying worst-case loop bounds blindly.

blocks.text: Across the complete scan, right advances n times and left advances at most n times. The work inside each update is constant, so the total is linear under the stated invariant.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.inner_constant: It can run many times, but the total is amortized.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorting_cost: The standard algorithm need not sort, and sorting adds cost.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.random_access: The proof charges each actual pointer movement once.
